tur57-0: Why does trigger finger happen, how is it recognised and graded, and does it go away on its own? The evidence for night splints, cortisone injections and surgery, a short history, trigger thumb in children, and six home techniques.
tur57-1: Trigger finger is when the tendon that bends a finger thickens and catches in the pulley it passes through: the finger stays bent and snaps with a "click" as it straightens. It can make using the hand difficult. Mild cases can improve with rest, a night splint and gentle movements; if not, there are options of an injection and a small operation.

tur57-5: The tendons that bend the fingers glide through small pulleys attached to the bone. When the tendon or its sheath swells and thickens, it catches at the mouth of the pulley; sometimes a small lump forms. As the finger bends, the lump passes through the pulley; as it straightens, it catches and then suddenly springs free, like a trigger being pulled and released.
tur57-6: A small lump at the base of the finger that moves with the finger
tur57-7: The diagnosis is made from your symptoms and an examination of your hand. The examination looks for tenderness in the palm at the base of the affected finger; sometimes a small lump that moves with the finger can be felt. Catching or snapping may be seen as the finger bends and straightens.
tur57-9: Pre-triggering stage: pain, a feeling of catching and tenderness at the base of the finger.
tur57-10: The finger catches, but you can straighten it yourself.
tur57-11: You can straighten the catching finger only with your other hand (IIIA), or you cannot fully bend the finger (IIIB).
tur57-12: Catching together with the middle joint of the finger staying permanently bent.
tur57-13: The grade is used to describe the findings. According to one study cited in a 2023 review, the higher the grade, the more likely a cortisone injection is to fail.
tur57-14: A night splint is very effective, especially in mild cases and when the finger catches at night: a short splint that limits movement at the base of the finger rests the tendon and pulley and helps prevent catching at night. It is worn through the night; a hand therapist can make one that suits you. Applying an anti-inflammatory gel to the base of the finger at night may also help; ask your physician which one is suitable.
tur57-15: A painkiller or anti-inflammatory gel for pain; ask your physician which one is suitable.
tur57-17: When other methods have not worked; a small procedure that releases the pulley.

tur57-28: From the first description to today's treatments
tur57-29: Trigger finger was described in the middle of the 19th century. In the 20th century a method of releasing the pulley under the skin was developed; reviews in recent years have compared the place of splints, injections and surgery.
tur57-30: Notta described the thickening in the finger-bending tendon that causes catching in four adult patients; this thickening is now known as "Notta's node".
tur57-31: Lorthioir described, in 52 patients, a method in which the pulley the tendon passes through is released under the skin without a large incision (percutaneous release).
tur57-32: Cochrane review: only two small studies (63 people) on cortisone injections were found; an injection with added cortisone was more effective than an injection containing only a numbing medicine.
tur57-33: Cochrane review (14 studies, 1,260 people): compared with a cortisone injection, open surgery may reduce recurrence at 6–12 months (low-quality evidence) but may cause more pain in the first week.
tur57-34: A review (SurgiColl): patient-reported success rates for splints ranged from 47% to 93%; success with a single cortisone injection ranged from 45% to 80%.
tur57-35: Put your hand in warm water and gently straighten your finger in the water. This makes it easier to straighten a catching finger. Do not force it.
tur57-37: Rub a little baby oil onto the base of your finger. Wrap an ice cube in cling film or a thin cloth and rub it firmly over the base of the finger until the ice melts. This helps reduce irritation in the area.
tur57-40: Using your good hand, gently close the fingers of the affected hand into a fist; the fingers themselves should not tense. Then let go.
tur57-41: Wear the splint your hand therapist gives you, or a short splint that limits movement at the base of the finger, through the night. The tendon and the pulley it passes through rest, and catching at night is prevented. If your skin reddens or the splint rubs, tell your therapist.

tur57-43: According to a 2023 review, success with a single cortisone injection ranges from 45% to 80% across studies; recent studies have found the injection to be similarly effective in people with diabetes. Randomised controlled trials, however, are few: a 2009 Cochrane review found two small studies of 63 people. According to the review's plain-language summary, 37 in 100 people benefited from an injection with added cortisone and 17 in 100 from an injection containing only a numbing medicine. According to the authors' conclusions, in one study the effect lasted up to 4 months. According to one study, the higher the grade of trigger finger, the more likely the injection is to fail.
tur57-44: Symptoms are often worse in the morning. If the finger catches at night, a short splint that limits movement at the base of the finger through the night is very effective. Putting your hand in warm water and gently straightening the finger in the water also makes it easier to open a catching finger; do not force it open.
tur57-45: How many injections can I have?
tur57-46: There is no fixed limit; your physician decides. In one study cited in a 2023 review, about 39% of second and third injections gave relief lasting at least 1.5 years. If catching persists despite injections, the option of surgery is discussed.
tur57-47: Does it happen in children too?
tur57-48: Yes. Trigger thumb or finger can appear in infancy and in older children; it is rarely noticed at birth. It is usually painless and does not stop the child using the hand. It can get better without treatment, but this can take 1–2 years; there is no evidence that splints or exercises make a difference. Surgery is done in the small number of children in whom it does not improve; NHS Fife's patient information page states that this operation is not done before the age of 3.
tur57-49: Most people do not need it. If other methods do not work, the pulley the tendon passes through is released with a small procedure. In a 2018 Cochrane review, recurrence was seen in about 7 in 100 people within 6–12 months after open surgery (low-quality evidence).

tur57-59: What is De Quervain's, how is it recognised and why is it common in new mothers? How long is a splint worn, do cortisone injections work, and when is surgery needed? A comparison of the evidence, a short history, six home exercises and videos.
tur57-60: Approximate proportion of working-age (18–65) women and men affected; more common in women, especially those with a young baby
tur57-61: The age range in which it is most common among working-age adults; it can occur at any age
tur57-62: 2023 network meta-analysis (1,663 patients): the best result for function came from a cortisone injection combined with a short period of splinting
tur57-64: The diagnosis is usually made from your symptoms and an examination. Two tendons that move the thumb pass over the bony bump on the thumb side of the wrist, through a tunnel under a roof of connective tissue; the examination looks for tenderness in this area and uses tests that stretch the tendons.
tur57-66: The physician holds your thumb and quickly bends your hand towards the little-finger side. Marked pain on the thumb side of the wrist supports the diagnosis.
tur57-68: You tuck your thumb into your palm and close your other fingers over it; the physician bends your wrist towards the little-finger side. Because it also stresses nearby structures, it can give a false-positive result.
tur57-70: An X-ray does not help with the diagnosis, but it may be taken to rule out other causes of wrist pain. Ultrasound is effective for diagnosis and for planning treatment; it can show whether there is a dividing wall (septum) splitting the tunnel in two. In studies, this wall is found in between 24% and 91% of people.
tur57-71: Conditions that can be confused with it
tur57-73: Arthritis of the joint at the base of the thumb, irritation where tendons cross in the forearm (intersection syndrome), irritation of the branch of the radial nerve under the skin (Wartenberg syndrome), trigger thumb, and a fracture of the scaphoid bone in the wrist or of the tip of the forearm bone (radius).
tur57-74: De Quervain's is about three times more common in women than in men, especially in those with a young baby. The reason is not fully known: hormonal changes during pregnancy and after birth, and repeatedly lifting, carrying and feeding the baby, may all play a part.
tur57-75: The movement that hurts most is bending the wrist sideways. So it is advisable to change the position of your hand and wrist during painful tasks, take frequent breaks from gripping tasks and avoid movements that bend the wrist sideways. When lifting and carrying your baby, also try to avoid movements that bend your wrist sideways.
tur57-76: Cooling the area for 20 minutes three times a day may reduce pain. Ask your physician which painkillers or anti-inflammatory medicines and gels are suitable.
tur57-77: If the splint and exercises are not enough, a cortisone injection into the sheath may be considered; some people need more than one injection. In a network meta-analysis published in 2023 covering 30 studies (1,663 patients), adding a short period of thumb splinting to an injection gave a slightly better result for function than the injection alone; a splint alone was among the least effective options for short-term pain. The authors recommended an injection followed by 3–4 weeks of splinting as first-line treatment; however, the certainty of the evidence was moderate for function and low or very low for pain. Surgery is rarely needed; in a day-case procedure the sheath is opened to give the tendons room.

tur57-91: The condition was described at the end of the 19th century; the tests used for diagnosis appeared in the first half of the 20th century. Studies in recent years have highlighted the combined use of injection and splinting.
tur57-92: Swiss surgeon Fritz de Quervain saw his first patient in December 1894 and published five cases in 1895; the condition now bears his name. De Quervain credited Kocher with the first description and the first operation.
tur57-93: De Quervain returned to the subject with eight new cases.
tur57-94: Eichhoff described the test in which the wrist is bent towards the little-finger side with the thumb inside the fist.
tur57-95: Finkelstein (JBJS) described the test in which the physician holds the patient's thumb and quickly bends the hand towards the little-finger side. The Eichhoff test is often wrongly called by his name.

tur57-98: Rest your forearm on a table and make a fist with your thumb pointing up, with your hand over the edge of the table. Slowly lower your wrist towards the floor, then bring it back up. Do it without a weight at first. When it becomes easy, hold a light weight; with a weight, do 3 sets of 12 every other day.
tur57-99: Without a weight: 10–15 reps, 4 times a day
tur57-100: Injections are widely used. A 2009 Cochrane review could find only one small study of 18 people. All participants were pregnant or breastfeeding women; pain went away completely in all nine women who had the injection and in none of the nine who wore only a splint. The authors stressed that the study was small and of poor methodological quality. In a network meta-analysis published in 2023 covering 30 studies (1,663 patients), the best results for function were seen in groups given an injection combined with a short period of thumb splinting; a splint alone was among the least effective options for short-term pain. The certainty of the evidence is moderate for function and low or very low for pain. Your physician will decide whether an injection is right for you.
tur57-101: Do I need an X-ray or ultrasound?
tur57-102: The diagnosis is usually made by examination. An X-ray does not help in diagnosing De Quervain's, but it can help rule out other causes of the pain. Ultrasound, however, can show thickening of the tendons, narrowing of the tunnel and whether a dividing wall (septum) splits the tunnel in two; it is useful for diagnosis and for planning treatment. If another cause of the pain is suspected, your physician may request other tests.
tur57-103: When does surgery come into question?
tur57-104: Surgery may be considered if there is no improvement within 3–6 months despite non-surgical treatment. In the operation, the tunnel the tendons pass through is opened to free the tendons. In one systematic review, symptoms resolved completely in up to 95% of patients after surgery. Having a dividing wall in the tunnel and a tendon made up of more than one slip have been linked to non-surgical treatment not working.
tur57-106: If you are still struggling after four weeks, see a physiotherapist or a physician.

tur57-110: Mechanical or inflammatory? Low back pain that starts slowly in young people and lasts for months is sometimes caused by axial spondyloarthritis, an inflammatory disease of the spine; ankylosing spondylitis is one form of this disease. According to the international ASAS criteria, in back pain lasting more than 3 months, inflammatory back pain is suspected if at least four of these five features are present: onset before age 40, an insidious and slow onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, and pain at night that eases on getting up. This is not a diagnosis and the criteria are not perfect; if you have these features, see a physician. Ankylosing spondylitis guide →
